```{r library, message = FALSE}
library(tidycreel)
```

## What this design is

The most common creel survey has two parts, collected separately:

- **Instantaneous counts** give effort. A clerk counts the anglers fishing at
  a moment, and that count stands for a period of time.
- **Interviews** give catch rates. The clerk asks parties how long they have
  fished and what they have caught.

A total is effort times rate. The interviews come in two kinds, and the only
difference in tidycreel is one argument, `interview_type`:

| | Access interviews | Roving interviews |
|---|---|---|
| Where the clerk is | At the access point, as parties leave | Moving through the fishery |
| Trips | Mostly complete | All incomplete: the party is still fishing |
| Catch rate | Ratio of means, complete trips | Mean of ratios, all trips but the shortest |
| `interview_type` | `"access"` (the default) | `"roving"` |

The counts, and so the effort, are the same either way. This page runs one
season's counts with each kind of interview. `vignette("tidycreel")` walks
through the access half step by step; this page is the short version, plus
roving.

## Design and counts

```{r design}
design <- creel_design(example_season_calendar, date = date, strata = day_type)
design <- add_counts(design, example_season_counts,
  count_col = total_anglers,
  period_length_col = daylight_hours
)
```

One count was made on each of the 36 sampled days, and it stands for the
14-hour fishing day, so `daylight_hours` is the period length. Effort for a day
is the count times that length, in angler-hours. Without `period_length_col`
the unit of effort is unknown and `estimate_effort()` warns.

## Effort

```{r effort}
estimate_effort(design, target = "period_total")
```

About 9,994 angler-hours over the 120-day season. `target = "period_total"`
asks for the season; the default, `"sampled_days"`, is the effort on the 36
days counted. Both kinds of interview below use this effort.

## Access interviews

```{r access}
access <- add_interviews(design, example_season_interviews,
  catch = catch_total,
  harvest = catch_kept,
  effort = hours_fished,
  trip_status = trip_status,
  n_anglers = n_anglers
)

estimate_catch_rate(access)
access_catch <- estimate_total_catch(access, target = "period_total")
access_catch
```

`interview_type` is left at `"access"`. The catch rate is a ratio of means
over the 172 complete trips: total catch divided by total angler-hours, about
0.22 fish per angler-hour. The 59 incomplete trips are left out, because a
party met while still fishing is more likely to be met the longer it stays.
Times about 9,994 angler-hours, that is about 2,230 fish.

## Roving interviews

```{r roving}
head(example_roving_interviews)

roving <- add_interviews(design, example_roving_interviews,
  catch = catch_total,
  harvest = catch_kept,
  effort = hours_fished,
  trip_status = trip_status,
  trip_duration = hours_fished,
  n_anglers = n_anglers,
  interview_type = "roving"
)
```

Every party in `example_roving_interviews` was still fishing, so `catch_total`
and `hours_fished` are the catch and the hours so far. `trip_duration` is the
time the party had fished when interviewed, which here is `hours_fished`.
tidycreel uses it to drop very short trips, below.

```{r roving-rate}
estimate_catch_rate(roving)
```

With `interview_type = "roving"`, tidycreel uses the mean-of-ratios estimator
of Hoenig et al. (1997) over all trips: each party's catch per angler-hour so
far, averaged. A ratio of means would be wrong here. A roving clerk meets long
trips more often than short ones, and the ratio of means gives those trips
more weight again. Averaging each party's own rate does not.

The warning is expected, and is the subject of this paragraph. A party
interviewed a few minutes into its trip has a catch rate that is mostly noise:
one fish in ten minutes is six fish an hour. By default trips that have fished
less than half an hour (`truncate_at = 0.5`, following Hoenig et al. 1997) are
left out of the rate, and tidycreel reports how many. Here it is
`r sum(example_roving_interviews$hours_fished < 0.5)` of
`r nrow(example_roving_interviews)` parties. The warning also suggests this
many short trips may be a data problem. It is not here: a clerk who meets
parties at random points in their trips meets some of them early. Check your
own data before deciding the same.

The rate is about 0.20 fish per angler-hour from the 183 parties that had
fished at least half an hour. The parties were simulated with a true catch
rate of 0.22 fish per angler-hour, inside the 95% confidence interval of 0.15
to 0.24.

```{r roving-totals}
roving_catch <- estimate_total_catch(roving, target = "period_total")
roving_catch
estimate_total_harvest(roving, target = "period_total")
```

The totals multiply the same season effort by the roving rates: about 1,960
fish caught and 630 kept. Each estimate built on a roving rate drops the short
trips again. The warning printed once for this design; each estimate still
records it, and `get_warnings(roving_catch)` lists it.

## Results as data

`as_tibble()` turns an estimate into a table with one row per estimate and the
metadata in columns. Binding the two catch totals shows them side by side:

```{r as-tibble}
totals <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    interviews = "access",
    tibble::as_tibble(access_catch)
  ),
  data.frame(
    interviews = "roving",
    tibble::as_tibble(roving_catch)
  )
)
totals[, c("interviews", "estimate", "se", "estimator", "unit")]
```

The two are different sets of interviews from the same days, so their totals
need not agree; they should be close when both kinds of interview describe the
same fishery.

## Plot

```{r plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Total catch on weekdays and weekends from the roving interviews, with 95 percent confidence intervals."}
ggplot2::autoplot(
  estimate_total_catch(roving, by = day_type, target = "period_total")
)
```

## References

Hoenig, J. M., Jones, C. M., Pollock, K. H., Robson, D. S., and Wade, D. L.
(1997). Calculation of catch rate and total catch in roving surveys of anglers.
*Biometrics* 53:306–317.

Pollock, K. H., Jones, C. M., and Brown, T. L. (1994). *Angler Survey Methods
and Their Applications in Fisheries Management.* American Fisheries Society
Special Publication 25.
